title: Establishing an Octopus Ecosystem for Biomedical and Bioengineering Research
protocol: Obtain all non-biological materials for an aquarium.
Wash tubing, piping, and filter system parts with 70% ethanol.
Rinse washed parts with deionized (DI) water.
Place a fiberglass table measuring 13 inches x 49 inches x ½ inch on the setup area.
Attach four carbon fiber legs measuring 2 inches x 2 inches x 23 inches under each corner of the tabletop.
Place 2-inch long carbon fiber stabilization braces between each leg, attached to the underside of the table.
Attach another shelf with the same dimensions directly on the ground below the table.
Let the pump sit directly on the bottom shelf surface.
Position the tank on the top surface of the fiberglass table.
Drill a single 1¾ inch hole, 2 inches from one side of the tank, using glass cutting drill bits.
Slide the end of the intended male PVC pipe into the end of the female pipe.
Place a piece of painters' tape on the outside of the male pipe that is still visible to prevent primer and cement from showing.
Separate the parts after taping and place a light coat of primer on the outside of the male pipe following application of cement in the same area.
Refit the male pipe into the female pipe as soon as possible after applying cement, then remove tape.
Wash out newly connected parts with DI water 24 hours after applying primer and cement.
Permanently connect the 1 inch outer diameter end of the suction screen to the 1 inch inner diameter end of the elbow joint.
Connect the end of the elbow joint to straight PVC tubing (1 inch OD).
Connect the other side of the straight tubing then to the 1 inch ID of the through-wall straight adapter female socket connector.
Permanently connect the through-wall straight adapter to a straight 4 inch long PVC pipe with a 1 inch OD.
Permanently connect the straight pipe to the center of the PVC connector (1 inch ID Tee shaped).
Permanently connect two 6 inch long pipes (1 inch OD) to both opposite ends of the tee connector-one facing directly up for the air release and the other directly down for water flow.
Permanently connect the downward extended straight pipe to a female socket barbed pipe (1-inch ID) straight adaptor.
Attach a 36 inches long rubber tube (¾ inch ID) to the barbed pipe adaptor.
Attach the ¾ inch barb fittings to the chiller unit's input and output ports.
Place the rubber tubing on the inlet fitting of the chiller.
Connect a new piece of ¾ inch ID tubing from the chiller output to the sump system inlet as shown in Figure 2b.
Place the 4 inch x 12 inch sock filter with pore size of 200 µm into its designated area as shown in Figure 2.
Place the protein skimmer and return pump into their appropriate areas.
Attach the automatic top off float valve to the inside wall of the pump area, 2 inches above the top of the pump's water inlet.
Permanently connect a straight 12-inch-long tube (¾ inch OD) to the pump's outlet.
Connect the other end of the 12-inch-long tube to a ¾ inch ID 45° elbow joint.
Connect the larger adapter end (2-inch OD) of the reducing adaptor permanently to the input of the UV light.
Match the placement of UV light inlet with the pump's output pipe so that the pipe is not bending between light and pump.
Drill holes into the stabilization brace to match the UV light attachment holes.
Attach the UV light to the table using screws matching the drill bit size.
Permanently connect the 2-inch side of another reducing adaptor to the output of the UV light.
Attach a 1-inch OD, 5-inch long straight tube to the adaptor's 1-inch ID.
Connect a 90° corner piece with the 1-inch ID to the 1-inch OD tube; direct unattached end toward water input side.
Permanently connect the other end of the corner piece to a 6 inches long tube (Part #69) having 1-inch OD with the input of the flow control unit (Part #2).
Permanently connect another 1-inch OD tube (Part #69) to the output of the flow monitoring unit; extend at least 3 inches beyond the side of the tank.
Cut a new hole 3 inches above the intended waterline and 2 inches away from the side of the tank on the opposite side to the one with water output.
Attach another through-wall bulkhead fitting with a 1-inch slip (Part #77) facing out of the tank.
Connect a straight tube with the 1-inch OD and 4 inches length permanently to the bulkhead.
Cut tubing from the last part of step 1.21 to match the distance this tubing extends from the tank.
Permanently connect a 90° tube to each of the open pipes.
Cut a final 1-inch OD straight tube that permanently connects both corner pieces.
Mount the power strip to the table or nearby wall.
Next to it, mount the fluid monitoring module.
Connect the flow sensor, power strip, and leak detection sensors to the module.
Set up the growth light attached to the algae bin.
Plug in the flow sensor, UV light, growth light, pump, and protein skimmer to the energy bar.
Prepare saltwater by mixing half a cup of commercially available salt mix with 1 gallon of reverse osmosis or deionized water.
Make 45 gallons of prepared saltwater to fully fill one tank and sump system.
Turn on the pump within the sump system flow controller.
Keep adding saltwater until the automatic top off valve is in the off position.
Fill the water in the tank until it is full.
Turn on the water chilling unit and set the temperature between 18 °C and 22 °C.
Turn on the protein skimmer.
Add 30 kg of crushed coral to the bottom of the tank.
Add a layer of crushed coral to the bottom of the algae bin.
Place multiple live rocks in the tank.
Add any other additions to the octopus environment.
Cover the opening of the tank with a top.
Add nitrifying bacteria as directed on the packaging.
Check daily for temperature, salinity, pH, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate levels using water testing kits.
Ensure ammonia levels are below 0.5 ppm.
Ensure nitrite levels are below 0.25 ppm.
Ensure nitrate levels are below 10 ppm.
Turn off UV light when adding nitrifying bacteria.
Reactivate the UV light once parameters are within safe ranges.
Check pH and oxygenation after system establishment, aiming for a range of 8.0-8.4 and appropriate oxygen levels.
Prior to adding animals, check for copper presence using a copper water testing kit.
Test the DI/RO water source for copper if it is found in the water.
Perform a 30% water change and place the activated carbon block within the water after confirming the water source does not contain copper.
Clean all parts and perform a full water change if the problem persists despite adding an activated carbon block.
Add 10 ghost shrimp into the system at least one week before adding octopuses to introduce biomass for bacteria and indicate overall water quality.
Add Chaetomorpha spp., Trochus Sp., and Mercenaria mercenaria to the algae bin.
Set up two tall 60-gallon water storage tanks, one for the saltwater and the other for RO water.
Attach a ¼ inch tubing to the automatic top of the float valve in the sump system.
Attach the other end of tubing to the bottom of the freshwater tank.
Fill the saltwater tank with water.
Add the proportional amount of salt to the tank.
Continuously aerate the saltwater storage tank for mixing and proper oxygenation.
Wait for one hour before use to ensure full mixing of the salt.
Transfer 8 gallons of matured saltwater to the shrimp tank one week after the octopus tanks are matured.
Add 15 kg of crushed coral to the bottom of the tank.
Add live rocks to the tank for hiding spots for molting.
Attach a cannister filter to the edge of the tank.
Set up the cannister filter as directed by the manufacturer.
Add an air pump next to the tank connected to a tube with an attached air stone put into the tank.
Clean the filter.
Change the filter pads every week.
Change 25% of the water weekly.
Check nitrogen parameters daily in food tanks.
Check pH parameters daily in food tanks.
Check temperature parameters daily in food tanks.
Perform additional water changes if necessary.
Add a nitrogen absorbent bag to the water if needed.
Move shrimp to a larger tank after one month if issues persist.
Remove shrimp from shipping water upon arrival.
Place shrimp in small saltwater tank for 5 minutes.
Directly add shrimp to the main tank after removal from shipping water.
Add mosquito fish directly to the shrimp tank on arrival.
Purchase shrimp and Mosquito fish from commercial suppliers as needed.
Feed shrimp and fish with fish flakes, dead vegetation, or algae.
Add 1 gallon of saltwater to the crab tank.
Add 10 kg of pebbles to the crab tank.
Pile pebbles in one side of the crab tank leaving dry land on the other side.
Maintain a water depth of 2 cm with saltwater for the crab tank.
Ensure salinity is between 30-35 ppt for optimal conditions.
Ensure temperature is between 22-25 °C for optimal conditions.
Add fiddler crabs directly into the tank.
Feed fiddler crabs once a day by adding fish flakes into the dish on the dry area of the tank.
Clean weekly by removing crabs and changing 100% of the saltwater.
Clean the pebbles.
Store marine bivalve mollusks within the saltwater tanks for the octopuses to open themselves.
Place mussels inside a separate unoccupied tank for the first week.
Ensure ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate levels are below 0.5 ppm, 0.25 ppm, and 10 ppm respectively before introducing the octopus.
Have water hand pump available to remove octopus ink from the tank.
It is recommended to have two people for this procedure.
On arrival, place the bag on the scale and subtract the weight of the bag after the octopus is removed.
Add an air stone to the bag to increase water oxygenation while transferring the animal to their tank.
Measure the shipping water's temperature and salinity.
Record cases of prolonged illness after shipment.
Hang the transport bag over the corner of the tank with the bag partially submerged in the tank water.
Remove 10% of the water from the bag and dump down the sink.
Add the same amount of water from the tank to the bag.
Repeat every 10 min until the temperature difference between the bag and the tank is no more than 1°.
Ensure gloves are worn when moving octopuses to their individual tanks.
Place both hands under the octopus to provide support during transfer.
Gently pull the suctioned arms from the side of the bag with a second person's assistance.
Move the octopus quickly into the water of its new habitat.
Use the hand pump to remove any ink released by the octopus when in the tank.
Weigh the bag with water to obtain an approximate weight of the animal.
Monitor the octopus' daily consumption, which should be around 4% to 8% of their weight for the first two weeks after arrival.
Check on the octopus four times a day during the first two weeks and then twice per day thereafter.
Weigh the octopus every two weeks to adjust food consumption as needed.
Place a 2.5 kg weight on the lid of the tank to prevent the octopus from escaping.
Use a commercially available saltwater testing kit for pH, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate.
Add the specified amount of tank water to each test tube provided with the kit.
Add the colorimetric reactant to the corresponding tubes as per kit instructions.
If ammonia levels are above 0.5 ppm, wash biomass out of the sock filter or change to a new sock filter.
If nitrite levels exceed 0.25 ppm and nitrate levels surpass 10 ppm, clean biomass from the top of the skimmer with a brush.
Add additional denitrifying bacteria to the tank if needed.
Replace 25% of fresh saltwater if problems persist despite cleaning measures.
Remove all dead crab and shrimp carcasses from the tank.
Remove octopus fecal matter using a hand pump.
Move all living crabs from the tank to the storage tank.
Rearrange large objects within the tank.
Introduce half the number of crabs that the octopus would eat daily, weighing 1.25 +/- 0.25 g.
Feed defrosted shrimp or small male fiddler crabs to juvenile octopuses.
Introduce five ghost shrimp daily to the tank.
Offer one live clam or mussel once a week.
Maintain three mosquito fish inside the tank at all times.
Provide frozen shrimp as a food source based on the octopus' weight.
Shut down the skimmer.
Turn off the pump.
Turn off the algae bin lights.
Turn off the automatic valve of the system.
Remove water only from the sump system.
Scrub algae bin lightly to remove biomass from its walls.
Clean the rest of the sump area with a brush.
Remove the sock filter.
Clean the sock filter with vinegar.
Let the sock filter dry.
Rotate sock filters weekly, replacing them every three months.
Remove and clean biomass from the top of the skimmer weekly.
Put the skimmer back into the system.
Begin refilling with saltwater.
Turn all systems back on when pump area is beginning to fill.
Stop adding water when the automatic float valve is in the off position.
Obtain a 6 L container with lid that is at least 15 cm tall.
Place 4 L of water directly from the octopus's tank into the container.
Provide aeration for 4 L of saltwater using a small air pump with air stone.
Add 1% EtOH to the container prior to octopus introduction.
Record the number of breaths per minute by counting the exhalation of water from the siphon before handling the octopus.
Record the octopus' skin pigmentation and baseline breathing rate prior to moving it.
Remove the octopus from the tank using a clean 4 L open mouth container by scooping it up with its surrounding water.
Weigh the octopus while in the container.
Move the octopus by placing both hands around its body and lifting it up.
Add a second person if needed to remove suctioned limbs from the container walls.
Quickly move the octopus into the prepared container with 1% EtOH.
Close the lid of the container to prevent escape.
Record the respiration of the octopus per minute by counting exhalation from siphon at the end of the first 5 min.
If the respiration remains above baseline and the animal continues to respond to a light pinch, add an additional 0.25% EtOH to water.
Continue adding ethanol to water up to a maximum of 3% EtOH.
Check for unconsciousness by observing loss of control over chromatophores.
Lightly pinch the arms to test for motor response and confirm unconscious state before proceeding with experiments.
Monitor the octopus' breathing and color under anesthesia.
Add 0.25% EtOH if the octopus begins to awaken during the procedure.
Transfer the octopus to a new tank of oxygenated water upon normal respirations and return of skin pigments.
Prepare a new 6 L container with 4 L of water from the octopus' holding tank for euthanasia.
Mix in MgCl2 to a concentration of 4% into the euthanasia tank.
Anesthetize the octopus following steps from 8.1 to 8.9.
Move the octopus after step 8.8 to the euthanasia tank.
Wait for breathing to stop and then wait an additional 5 minutes.
Perform decerebration of the octopus or keep it in the euthanasia tank for 5 more minutes after initial cessation of breathing.
Do not feed the octopus on mornings when training with a screw cap container is planned.
Set up a camera recording device pointing at the feeding area.
Obtain a 50 mL screw cap tube with 1 mm diameter holes throughout the surface and the cap for water flow.
Place a fiddler crab within the container.
Add a weight inside the container or attach it externally to ensure the container remains at the bottom of the tank.
Submerge the container in the tank, ensuring it is visible to both the octopus and the camera.
Remove the crab from the tube if not eaten after 4 hours.
Resume regular feeding schedule for the day.
Repeat the exercise daily.
Obtain MRI images using a 7T system.
Wrap the euthanized octopus in kitchen-grade polyvinyl chloride plastic wrap to maintain tissue hydration.
Place the octopus on the wrap, tuck in the ends, and roll to seal.
Use a volume transmit/receive coil with a 4 cm diameter for imaging the brain and multiple arms.
Acquire T1 weighted RARE sequence images of the rodent brain using parameters: TR = 1500 ms, TE = 20 ms, resolution = 117 x 117 x 500 µm, 100 averages, RARE factor = 8.
Image the octopus arm with an 86 mm volume transmit coil and a 4 x 4 cm 4-channel array receive coil.
Cut off an octopus arm using surgical scissors.
Place the cut arm in a 15 mL conical tube filled with phosphate-buffered saline.
Use T1 weighted inversion recovery sequence (MP-RAGE) for imaging with parameters: TR/TE = 4000/2.17 ms, inversion delay = 1050 ms, resolution = 100 x 100 x 500 µm, 9 averages.
Flash-freeze the octopus in a fume hood.
Cover the bottom of a Dewar with dry ice and fill it with hexanes.
Slowly lower the octopus into the hexanes over about 10 min.
Add fresh hexanes and dry ice as required to fully cover the octopus with cold hexanes.
Keep the frozen octopus at -20 °C until embedding.
Embed and section the octopus:
Create a rectangular mold using tools provided by the CFT manufacturer.
Cover the bottom of the mold with OCT media and freeze to a semi-solid gel.
Place the frozen octopus into the gel layer of the OCT.
Cover the octopus slowly with OCT in 2-3 layers, freezing between each step until the OCT is at the gel stage.
Freeze the block containing the entire octopus for at least 12 hours at -20 °C.
Load the sample into the cryo-fluorescence tomography system.
Section and image the entire euthanized O. bimaculoides at mesoscopic resolution using 3 emission/excitation filters, producing several 3D isotropic datasets.
Transfer sections to slides when sectioning reaches the arm and digestive system for further histology.
Load the raw dataset into reconstruction software from the CFT vendor designed for fast processing.
Reconstruct a 3-dimensional stack using landmark alignment, histogram balancing, fluorescence corrections and normalization, including removal of subsurface fluorescence effects for each wavelength.
